Plan by age · Stage 4 of 5

Ages 60–62: Decision years

This is when the big, hard-to-reverse decisions cluster: when to stop working, how to cover health insurance until Medicare, whether to convert pretax savings to Roth, and when to claim Social Security.

The decisions interact. A Roth conversion raises income, which can cut Marketplace subsidies now and raise Medicare premiums later. Claiming Social Security early locks in a smaller check for you and possibly for a surviving spouse. Work through them together, not one at a time.

The 60–63 super catch-up

What's happening

For the four calendar years you turn 60, 61, 62 and 63, the workplace catch-up limit is higher. If you are still working, it is the biggest tax-advantaged saving window you will get.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Saving the maximum versus retiring a year or two earlier.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming payroll will raise the limit automatically. Many plans require a new election.
  • Keeping the higher deferral in the year you turn 64, when the limit drops back.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $11,250Super catch-up (ages 60–63)2026, instead of the $8,000 standard catch-up, for a total of $35,750.Source: IRS: 2026 401(k) and IRA limits (IR-2025-111)

Your retirement date and the Roth conversion window

What's happening

Between your last paycheck and the start of Social Security and required minimum distributions, taxable income can be unusually low. Converting some pretax savings to Roth in those years can lower lifetime taxes, but every conversion also raises this year's income.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • How much to convert each year, if any.
  • Retire earlier and convert more, or work longer.

Common mistakes

  • Converting so much in one year that you lose health subsidies or jump an IRMAA tier.
  • Waiting until RMDs start, when the low-income window has closed.

Key numbers for 2026

  • age 73Required minimum distributionsRMDs generally begin at 73 under current rules.Source: IRS: Required minimum distribution FAQs
  • 2 yearsIRMAA look-backMedicare premiums are based on your tax return from two years earlier.Source: Medicare.gov: 2026 Medicare costs (incl. IRMAA table)

Healthcare bridge before Medicare

What's happening

If you stop working before 65, you need coverage until Medicare starts. Marketplace premium tax credits depend on your income for the year, and for 2026 coverage there is no credit above 400% of the federal poverty level.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • COBRA's continuity versus a Marketplace plan's subsidy.
  • How Roth conversions and capital gains fit under the income limit.

Common mistakes

  • Crossing 400% of the poverty level by a small amount and losing the whole credit.
  • Forgetting that a Roth conversion counts as income for the subsidy.

Key numbers for 2026

  • 100%–400% FPLPremium tax credit income rangeFor 2026 coverage the enhanced credits expired; above 400% there is no credit.Source: IRS: Premium tax credit questions and answers
  • $62,600 / $84,600400% of the poverty levelFor 2026 Marketplace coverage, household of 1 / 2 (lower 48 states).Source: CMS: 2026 Marketplace tax credit rules and FPL table
  • generally 18 monthsCOBRA continuationFrom the date job-based coverage would end.Source: U.S. Department of Labor: COBRA FAQs

Social Security: 62, full retirement age or 70

What's happening

You can claim from 62, but the check is permanently smaller. Waiting past full retirement age adds delayed retirement credits until 70. For married couples, the higher earner's choice also sets the survivor benefit.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Claim early, at full retirement age or at 70.
  • Which spouse claims first.

Common mistakes

  • Claiming at 62 by default because it is the first date available.
  • Ignoring how long a surviving spouse may rely on the larger check.

Key numbers for 2026

  • 70% of fullBenefit at 62For anyone born in 1960 or later, whose full retirement age is 67.Source: SSA: Starting your retirement benefits early
  • up to age 70Delayed retirement creditsWaiting past full retirement age raises the monthly benefit until 70.Source: SSA: Delayed retirement credits
  • $24,480Earnings test2026: below full retirement age, $1 is withheld for every $2 earned above this.Source: SSA: 2026 COLA fact sheet

Spousal and survivor benefits

What's happening

A spouse who earned less may collect up to half of the other spouse's full benefit. When one spouse dies, the survivor generally keeps the larger of the two checks. These rules make the claiming decision a household decision.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Whether the higher earner delays to raise the survivor benefit.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a spouse with little work history gets nothing.
  • Not reporting a death to SSA promptly, which delays survivor payments.

Key numbers for 2026

  • up to 50%Spousal benefitOf the worker's full-retirement-age benefit; reduced if claimed early.Source: SSA: Family (spousal) benefits
  • from age 60Survivor benefitsReduced if taken before the survivor's full retirement age.Source: SSA: Social Security if your spouse passes away

What's coming next

Ages 63–65: Medicare countdown

Medicare at 65 is the last big deadline before retirement settles into a routine. Income from two years earlier sets your Medicare premiums, so the planning starts at 63. Missing the enrollment window can mean penalties that last as long as you have Medicare.
